questions.q: What does Event ID 4624 represent in the Security log?
options: A member was added to a security group
A user account was created
An account failed to log on
An account was successfully logged on
questions.explain: 4624 fires every time a logon succeeds, interactive or not — it's the most common Security-log event on any active machine.

questions.q: In a 4624 event, what does the Logon Type field tell you?
options: Whether the logon was interactive (type 2), over the network (type 3), or via RDP (type 10)
Whether the account is an administrator or a standard user
The exact password length used
The physical location of the machine
questions.explain: Logon Type turns a 4624 from noise into a lead — the same Event ID tells very different stories depending on whether it's type 2, 3, or 10.

questions.q: A burst of 4625 events against the same account, or the same account failing from many different machines, most strongly suggests what?
options: A routine software update
A new user account being created
A successful administrator logon
A password-guessing or brute-force attempt
questions.explain: 4625 is the failure twin of 4624 — a repeated pattern of failures is the signature SOC alerting rules are built to catch.

options: A failed logon attempt
Special, administrator-equivalent privileges were assigned to a new logon
A group policy was refreshed
A user account was deleted
questions.explain: 4672 fires when an account logs on with admin-equivalent rights — not alarming alone, but worth escalating when paired unexpectedly with a 4624.

questions.q: Why is the sequence 4720, then 4728, then 4672 for the same account considered a textbook suspicious pattern?
options: Each of those IDs individually requires no further investigation
It simply means a printer driver was installed
It shows a new account created, then added to a privileged group, then logging on with elevated rights — a pattern consistent with someone quietly provisioning themselves admin access
It always indicates a scheduled Windows Update
questions.explain: Watched together, account creation, privileged-group membership, and an elevated logon is exactly the pattern of an attacker or insider provisioning persistent admin access.
